newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Bharti unit eyes global roaming.
newsitem.headline: India's Bharti unit eyes global roaming.

text.p: Bharti Cellular Ltd, a unit of Bharti Telecom Ltd, hopes to be the first Indian cellular operator to launch international roaming services, a senior company official said on Monday.

"We hope to start offering the service latest by September this year. We are waiting for a clearance from the Department of Telecommunications," Bharti Cellular executive director Anil Nayyar Ltd told Reuters.
He said that the company, which sells its service under the Airtel name, had received clearance from the Reserve Bank of India to make U.S. dollar payments for these services.
"We will now set up a separate bank account for receiving and making dollar payments," he said.

Bharti Telecom holds a controlling stake in Bharti Cellular, while British Telecom Plc (BT) and Italy's Stet Spa hold minority stakes. The joint venture operates India's largest cellular network in Delhi with 92,000 subscribers.

Nayyar said that Bharti Cellular is now waiting for the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) to implement the required signalling protocols needed to connect Bharti's exchange with those of its overseas roaming partners.
"We have implemented the signalling, and have tested it between Delhi and Bombay. What is left is for DoT to implement it between its exchange and that of VSNL," he said.
Videsh Sanchar Nigam Ltd (VSNL) is the state-controlled monopoly international carrier for India.

Nayyar said a clearinghouse was also in the offing, as a letter of intent had been signed between the Cellular Operators Association of India and Mach, a subsidiary of Luxembourg's Millicom International Cellular SA.
"Mach will set up the clearinghouse, and all cellular operators in India will pay one to two percent of the value of each roaming call as a fee," he said.
A clearing-house is an independent computer centre that monitors all roaming traffic and calculates the payments to be made or received by cellular operators with roaming subscribers.
Nayyar said that international roaming services would start first with BT, Stet and Millicom. "We will have to sign agreements with each different operator to extend this service."
He said that a roaming subscriber would pay 15 to 20 percent extra per minute, apart from a flat fee for the facility.

On roaming revenues, he said that there was no precedent to go by for India. "We expect roaming revenues to conform to international levels. In a mature network, 15 percent to 20 percent of the revenues come from roaming."
